title: The Grain Offering: A Gift from the Harvest
summary: A worshiper may bring a grain offering of fine flour with olive oil and frankincense, either raw or baked in an oven, cooked on a griddle, or prepared in a pan. The priest burns a handful as a memorial portion on the altar, and the rest belongs to the priests as most holy food. No leaven or honey may be burned on the altar, every grain offering must be seasoned with the salt of the covenant, and firstfruits of new grain are offered roasted and crushed.
story: Leviticus began with the burnt offering, in which a whole animal went up to God. Chapter 2 turns to the grain offering, the second of the five main offerings described in chapters 1 to 5. It is the only one of them that involves no animal and no blood, and the text never says that it makes atonement. It is a gift from the fruit of the land and the work of human hands: grain grown, ground, mixed with oil, and sometimes baked. In practice it often accompanied the burnt offering and the peace offering (Numbers 15:1-10), so that meat and bread, the whole of an ancient meal, were given to God. Chapter 3 goes on to the peace offering, the shared meal.
historical:
Grain, olive oil, and wine were the staple products of the land of Israel, and the grain offering drew on the first two. Fine flour was the best part of the wheat, probably what is now called semolina, and was more costly than ordinary meal. Frankincense, a resin from trees that grow in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, had to be imported along long caravan routes and was expensive. So even a bloodless offering could represent real value.

The instructions assume life in a settled agricultural land with harvests, ovens, and firstfruits, and they look ahead to Israel's life in Canaan. Traditional readers take them as given at Sinai for the life to come; many critical scholars see the priestly laws as reflecting the practice of the later temple. Either way, the grain offering was a lasting part of Israel's worship: an evening grain offering accompanied the daily sacrifice at the temple, and Elijah prayed on Mount Carmel at the time of the evening offering (1 Kings 18:36). The Jewish afternoon prayer is still called Minchah after it.
cultural:
The three cooking methods reflect ordinary kitchens. The oven (verse 4) was a clay cylinder heated from inside, with dough pressed against its walls, a kind still used in villages across the Middle East. The griddle (verse 5) was a flat plate of clay or metal set over a fire. The pan of verse 7 was probably a deeper vessel. The worshiper's own bread, baked in his own way, could be brought to God.

Only a handful was burned, the memorial portion, meaning the part that brought the worshiper to God's remembrance. The rest went to the priests as most holy food, to be eaten in the sanctuary (6:16). Priests had no inheritance of land (Numbers 18:20), and the people's offerings were their livelihood. Salt was a symbol of permanence and loyalty in the ancient Near East, because it preserves and because those who shared salt at a meal were bound to one another; in Ezra 4:14 royal officials cite their obligation to the palace in similar terms. Numbers 18:19 calls God's permanent grant of holy offerings to the priests a covenant of salt. Leaven and honey (probably fruit syrup as well as bees' honey) were excluded from the altar fire, perhaps because both involve fermentation and decay, though they could be brought as firstfruits (verse 12), as the leavened loaves at the Feast of Weeks were (23:17).
literary: The chapter is organized as a series of cases. It begins in the third person with uncooked flour (verses 1-3) and then shifts to direct address, if you bring, for baked, griddled, and pan-cooked offerings (verses 4-7). A summary of procedure (verses 8-10) repeats the key phrases of verses 2 and 3 almost exactly: the memorial portion, the pleasing aroma, and the remainder that belongs to Aaron and his sons as “a most holy part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD.” Then come general rules on leaven, honey, and salt (verses 11-13), and finally a special case, the firstfruits of new grain (verses 14-16). The repeated refrain, it is a grain offering (verses 6 and 15), marks each variation as equally legitimate.

outline.t: An offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense
Grain offerings baked, griddled, or cooked in a pan
How the priest presents it and the priests' share
No leaven or honey; always salt

doctrines.note: Every grain offering had to carry “the salt of the covenant of your God” (verse 13). Salt, which preserves, marked the relationship between God and Israel as lasting. Each ordinary offering of bread was a reminder that the worshiper stood inside a permanent covenant.

The grain offering returns to God a portion of what he gave through the land: rain, harvest, and the ability to work. By bringing the fruit of their labor, worshipers confessed that their daily bread came from him.

Most of the offering went to feed the priests, who had no land of their own. Gifts to God supported those who served him on the people's behalf, a pattern the New Testament applies to supporting those who minister (1 Corinthians 9:13-14).

words.note: Minchah, offering or gift, here the grain offering. In ordinary use it means a gift or tribute presented to a superior: Jacob's present to Esau (Genesis 32:13) and tribute paid to kings are called minchah. Cain's and Abel's offerings are both called by this name (Genesis 4:3-4). In Leviticus it names the gift of grain in particular.

Azkarah, memorial portion, related to the verb zakhar, to remember. The handful burned on the altar stood for the whole offering and brought the worshiper to God's remembrance. The Septuagint translated it with a Greek word meaning memorial, the same word used in Acts 10:4 when an angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God.

Melach, salt. Required on every grain offering (verse 13) and, according to the end of the verse, on all offerings. The phrase covenant of salt appears in Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5 for a covenant that lasts. Salt's power to preserve made it a natural picture of faithfulness that does not spoil.

Chamets, leaven or something leavened. It is excluded from the altar here and from Israel's houses during the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Exodus 12:15). Because leaven spreads through dough and works by fermentation, it later became a picture of corrupting influence, as in Jesus' warning about the leaven of the Pharisees and Paul's image in 1 Corinthians 5.

christ: The grain offering was a gift of bread from the harvest, and the New Testament speaks of Christ and of Christian life in similar terms, though it nowhere interprets this chapter directly. Jesus calls himself the bread of life (John 6:35) and speaks of his own death as a kernel of wheat that falls into the ground and dies so that it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Paul uses the image of unleavened bread for a life purified in Christ: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,” so believers are to keep the feast “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth” (1 Corinthians 5:7-8). Jesus calls his disciples the salt of the earth (Matthew 5:13). And the grain offering's character as a gift without blood reappears in the New Testament's language about Christian giving and praise: Paul calls the Philippians' gifts “a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18), and Hebrews urges believers not to neglect doing good and sharing, “for with such sacrifices God is pleased” (Hebrews 13:16).
questions: The grain offering brought the ordinary work of farming and baking to God. What part of your daily work could you offer to him as a gift?
Every offering had to include the salt of the covenant. What reminds you, in ordinary moments, that you belong to God for good?
Most of the offering fed the priests. How do your gifts to God support the people who serve others in his name?
